summary:
A visitor in the Basque Country stands under the national framework of Spain. Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the Law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGBTI persons, appeared in the Boletín Oficial del Estado (no. 51) on 1 March 2023 and applies uniformly across Spain's autonomous communities. The Basque Country's own instruments operate alongside it rather than displacing it.

Title II allows any person aged 16 or over to rectify the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry by simple declaration, with no requirement of prior medical diagnosis or treatment. That administrative route replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment, and rectification carries corresponding adaptation of identity documents. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, a provision that proved contentious, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination: the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Spain. This contrasts with the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines, where restrictions are applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime, and the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. Protection runs through the hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, which provide one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months and derive from Organic Law 6/2022. Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

The same statute bans non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expands assisted reproduction rules, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthens sexuality education, and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation. Human Rights Watch, reporting the Congress of Deputies' passage of the bill on 16 February 2023, places the reform within European and international standards against disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.
tangentialFactors:
Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay, all of which operate routes to legal gender recognition without medical prerequisites.

A 2016 survey of 23 countries ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change. The finding predates Ley 4/2023 and functions as a dated baseline rather than a measure of the current regime.

Public opinion in the region is documented at one point only: a 2017 survey by the Basque Youth Observatory reported that nine in ten Basque young people favour same-sex marriage and legal change of sex.

Institutional markers with a bearing on the local environment include the first Basque Pride march in Bilbao in 1978, the legalisation of the activist collective EHGAM in 1983, and the creation of Emakunde, the Basque Women's Institute, in 1988.
localsOnly:
The Basque Parliament passed a law in 2013 against discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognising the rights of trans people. It was the first instrument to incorporate an LGTBI perspective into gender-violence prevention in the Basque education system.

The Basque Country operates its own non-discrimination legal instruments and equality institutions, including Emakunde, within the national framework, so residents have a regional avenue of complaint in addition to the national one.

Osakidetza, the Basque health service, has provided assisted reproduction regardless of sexual orientation and reaffirmed that position in 2013.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents an enforcement action, penalty or complaint brought under the Basque Parliament's 2013 anti-discrimination law; the record of that instrument's use is unresolved.

Whether any Basque court has applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance is not sourced. The two documented applications are the Vigo misdemeanour case of July 2026 and the Valencia juvenile case reported on 8 January 2026, both outside this region.

No material addresses complaints, refusals or litigation over access to sex-separated facilities in the Basque Country; the facility rule is stated as law, not as observed practice.

Osakidetza guidance specific to trans healthcare, including waiting times or referral routes, is not sourced here.

The 2016 cross-country survey and the 2017 Basque Youth Observatory poll both predate Ley 4/2023 and cannot be read as measures of opinion under the current law.
